summary: blood urea nitrogen is what the Plasma osmolality calculator works out, and it gets there from the sodium, the glucose and the plasma osmolality. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Plasma osmolality calculator calculator work?
sections.html:
The Plasma osmolality calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports blood urea nitrogen in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the sodium, the glucose and the plasma osmolality.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A number, expressed in mEq/L.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams per decilitre. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milliOsmoles per kilogram of water. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Plasma osmolality calculator calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Blood urea nitrogen=-7 ÷ 45 × glucose + (14 ÷ 5) × plasma osmolality − 28 ÷ 5 × sodium

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Sodium = 10 and Glucose = 10 Mg/d l. The calculator returns Blood urea nitrogen = -29.5556 Mg/d l and Plasma osmolality = 10 mOsm/kg H₂O.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Blood urea nitrogen = -29.5556 Mg/d l and Plasma osmolality = 10 mOsm/kg H₂O should be roughly the size you expected from Sodium = 10 and Glucose = 10 Mg/d l.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in milligrams per deciliter, and convertible to any of the 2 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Glucose levels, opening in milligrams per decilitre
  • Bun – blood urea nitrogen, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • Osmolality, opening in milliOsmoles per kilogram of water

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Plasma osmolality calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the sodium, the glucose and the plasma osmolality — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Plasma osmolality calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Plasma osmolality calculator calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns blood urea nitrogen, derived from the sodium, the glucose and the plasma osmolality. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Plasma osmolality calculator calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the sodium, the glucose and the plasma osmolality, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter glucose in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Glucose opens in milligrams per decilitre and the chip beside it offers 2 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Blood urea nitrogen = -29.5556 Mg/d l. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Plasma osmolality calculator calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
